title: The terminal is a conversation
summary: You type a line, the computer answers in text: exactly, and the same way every time. Claude Code has this conversation for you.
note: Names, companies and files here are **made-up examples**.

props.title: Same input, same result
props.body: Every time. It reads the folder or file fresh, so it has no memory to get wrong, and it can't invent an answer.

props.text: What does my notes file say?
It says to call Acme on **Friday**.

props.title: Very likely, not guaranteed
props.body: Claude answers from what it has read and what's most likely. Usually right; sometimes out of date or wrong.

props.title: Have the conversation yourself
props.expect: Open **Terminal** (press ⌘ Space and type *Terminal*). Type `ls` and press Return: it lists the folders in your home folder. Then try `ls Documnets`, misspelled, and read its reply.

steps.title: You type, it answers
steps.text: On a Mac, the **Terminal** app is a text conversation with your computer. You type one line, a **command**, and press Return. It replies in text. Here, `ls` asks: *what's in this folder?*

steps.title: Very literal
steps.text: It does exactly what you typed, never what you meant. One swapped letter and there is no such folder, so it says so instead of guessing.

lines.text: ls: Documnets: No such file or directory

steps.title: Same input, same result
steps.text: Ask the same thing twice and you get the same answer, as long as nothing in the folder changed. Programmers call this **deterministic**.

steps.title: No memory to get wrong
steps.text: `cat` prints a file. It reads the file **fresh** every time, so after you edit it, the answer changes with it. And when a file isn't there, it can't make one up.

lines.text: (you edit the file and save it)
cat: Documents/todo.txt: No such file or directory

steps.title: Claude works differently
steps.text: Claude read your notes earlier, before you edited them. Asked now, it answers from what it read: confident, and out of date. Claude is **probabilistic**: very likely right, not guaranteed.

steps.title: So Claude checks
steps.text: Claude Code can run commands itself, in a **shell** (the program that runs commands) that it starts on your Mac, not in your Terminal window. When it checks the file instead of relying on memory, it gets the real answer, not a likely one.

claude.text: Let me check the file. It says to call Acme on **Monday**.

steps.title: The best of both
steps.text: Claude brings judgment: what to look for and what it means. The terminal brings exact answers. Knowing which is which is the theme of every explainer that follows.
